post.summary:
Where AWS Marketplace sends the buyer immediately after purchase.
            
             Three things about this endpoint are load bearing and easy to get wrong. AWS sends a POST, not a normal
             page visit. The token arrives as a form field in the request body despite being named like an HTTP
             header. And nothing is provisioned here — AWS does not honour resources created before the lifecycle
             notification arrives, so this only stages the licence and hands the buyer onward.

Completes signup for a buyer who arrived from AWS Marketplace. Called by the dashboard with the
            one-time token from the fulfillment redirect plus the details the buyer typed.

Where EventBridge delivers AWS Marketplace lifecycle notifications — upgrades, renewals and
             cancellations. The only channel through which a purchase can change after onboarding.
            
             Kept to authenticate, capture, publish, acknowledge. An API destination gives up on a slow endpoint and
             counts it as a delivery failure, so the licence read, the entitlement re-read and the client update all
             happen on the bus instead. Only the fields EventBridge guarantees are read here; the marketplace
             identifiers inside "detail" are parsed by the consumer, against the body persisted alongside them.

get.summary:
Returns the whole multi-currency settings section in one call: the feature toggle, the base currency taken
from the General points rule, and every configured currency. The list is returned even while the feature is
off, because turning the toggle off keeps the saved rates and the screen must still render them.

post.summary:
Configures an additional currency with its rate. The code and the rate are validated in the manager against
the ISO dataset, the base currency and the already configured codes, so an unusable value comes back as a
precise business status code (unsupported / is base / already configured / invalid rate), not a binding error.

put.summary:
Replaces the whole list of additional currencies with the submitted array in one write. Rows equal to the
stored ones keep their audit fields, new or re-rated rows are stamped with the acting user and time, and codes
left out are removed. Bound to the bare route, so it never collides with "toggle" or "{currencyCode}".

Turns the multi-currency feature on or off for the workspace. Routed to the general settings manager because
the flag lives on ClientGeneralSetting, and it moves the flag only — the configured rates are never touched,
so the merchant gets the same configuration back when the feature is switched on again. The literal "toggle"
segment is matched ahead of the "{currencyCode}" PUT below, since routing always prefers a literal segment.

Updates the rate of an already configured currency. Only the rate is read from the body — the currency being
edited is identified by the route so a mismatched body code can never silently re-price a different currency.
The acting user is stamped on the row because a rate edit re-prices every reward the merchant hands out.

delete.summary:
Removes a configured currency. There is no row and no delete of any kind here: the configured currencies
are entries in the Rates list of the ClientGeneralSetting.MultiCurrency jsonb blob, so the manager writes
back a newly projected list with that code left out, leaving the toggle and every other rate untouched.
            
Read this before adding another write path for these entries: the old unique (ClientId, CurrencyCode)
index is GONE with the table, so the database no longer refuses a duplicate currency. ClientCurrencyRules
.Validate, called inside ClientCurrencyManager, is now the ONLY thing standing between a workspace and two
entries for the same code carrying different rates — from which ResolveRate would take whichever happens
to come first in the list and price real orders with it. A writer that skips that validation, or that
appends to the list without it, reintroduces that silently at full production volume.
